children: Iron ore futures fell on Tuesday, snapping a four-day gaining streak, as a weak near-term demand outlook weighed on the market and a stronger yuan added more pressure on the yuan-denominated contract.
The most-traded January iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
traded 1.05% lower at 708 yuan ($105.70) a metric ton.
The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange was 1.19% higher at $95.85 a ton.

End-use demand has yet to reach a turning point, and iron ore demand is unlikely to improve in the near term and prices are likely to stay rangebound with a weaker bias, analysts from Shanghai Metals Market said in a note.

China's domestic steel demand will fluctuate downwards over the next decade, though it will likely remain above 800 million tons during the 15th Five-Year Plan before falling below that level by 2035, Liu Jian, president of the China Iron and Steel Association, said on Sunday.

China's yuan climbed to a 3-1/2-year high against the dollar on Tuesday after the central bank set a firmer daily fixing for the 10th straight session, the longest streak since late 2023, while investors awaited a meeting between the leaders of the world's two largest economies later this week.
A stronger currency makes yuan-denominated assets less affordable to overseas buyers.
Other steelmaking ingredients on the DCE rose, with coking coal
Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange were mixed. Rebar
